paras: The threatened lynching of Dick Dent was a manhunt in Winchester, Ohio, at the end of January 1888, in which the white population searched for Dent, a Black man accused of seduction, and was reported ready to lynch him if he was caught. No report of his capture appears in the coverage, which consists of one wire dispatch reprinted in papers from Ohio to California.

According to a Winchester dispatch dated January 31, Jennie Darlington, a sixteen-year-old farmer's daughter, swore out a warrant that morning charging Dent with seduction. She had first obtained a warrant against a school teacher named Nichols, whom the dispatch called "innocent", but then said she had done so "under threats of violence from Dent." The Springfield Daily Republic described Dent as "a colored man of family" and the girl as a "white farmer's pretty daughter."

Dent fled before he could be arrested, and the dispatch reported "great excitement" in the town over his flight. "The white population are all out searching for the fugitive," it said, adding that "if the negro is caught he will be lynched." The St. Paul Daily Globe's version said he would be "hanged to the nearest tree," and the Springfield paper reported that telegrams were being sent "all over the country to apprehend him."
No report of Dent's capture, arrest, trial or death was found, nor any further word on Darlington or Nichols.

The Washington Critic carried the earliest item on January 31, a single line in its "Condensed Telegrams" calling Dent "a colored tough" fleeing "from an indignant community." The full dispatch ran on February 1 in the Beatrice Daily Express and the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian under the headline "Excited Over an Absent Negro," and in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "The Whites Are Indignant." The Springfield Daily Republic, the only Ohio paper found, headed its version "A Hemp Cravat Awaits a Fugitive Negro," and the Mitchell Capital in Dakota used "A Wicked Coon Wanted" on February 3.
Every version repeated Darlington's accusation as stated and presented the coming lynching as an expected outcome rather than a crime. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The full dispatch gave the charge as seduction, while the Washington Critic said Dent had "assaulted a farmer's" (the item is cut off there) and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union said the warrant charged him "with assault." The Sacramento brief also placed the town in North Carolina and the Springfield paper printed the girl's age as "only 10," details that every other version gives as Ohio and sixteen.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Dick Dent
bases: The dispatch reports a search for a Black man accused of seduction by the white population of Winchester and says he would be lynched if caught, a threatened lynching (A2, A4, A5).
The papers report only a manhunt by the white population and a prediction that Dent would be lynched or hanged 'to the nearest tree' if caught; no capture or killing is reported (A2, A4, A5).
Every report is a version of one Winchester wire dispatch of Jan. 31 (A2, A4, A5), with condensed briefs (A1, A6); no independent or local account or follow-up was found.

accounts.label: Wire report from Winchester
accounts.gist: Dent fled after Jennie Darlington swore out a seduction warrant; she had first accused a teacher named Nichols, which she said she did under threats from Dent; the white population was searching and would lynch him if caught.

accounts.label: Ohio version (Springfield)
accounts.gist: Dated Feb. 1, it calls Dent a man of family, omits the Nichols warrant, says he would be 'swung from the nearest tree', and adds that telegrams were sent across the country to apprehend him.

accounts.label: Condensed briefs
accounts.gist: Short items describe Dent as fleeing an 'indignant community' after an assault and give the charge as assault.

framing.detail: Papers in Nebraska, Dakota, Minnesota and California ran the dispatch as a brief, reporting the lynching threat as an expected outcome ('If the negro is caught he will be lynched') without comment.
Headlines such as 'The Whites Are Indignant', 'A Hemp Cravat Awaits a Fugitive Negro' and 'A Wicked Coon Wanted' and the label 'a colored tough' cast the coming lynching as a natural response.

versions.value: assault ('assaulted a farmer's' [cut off]; 'charging him with assault')

conflicts.note: The full dispatch says seduction; the two briefs are condensed and likely paraphrase it.
Every other version, including the Ohio paper, places it in Ohio; the Sacramento brief appears garbled.
The Springfield figure is likely a typesetting or OCR error for 16.
